items.title: How to follow Las Vegas Grand Prix on the BBC
items.content: <article>All the key BBC coverage details for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, which takes place from 20-22 November.</article>
items.lbText:
The final triple header of the 2026 Formula 1 season starts in the United States with the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Lando Norris claimed his third victory of the season last time out in Sao Paulo, beating the Red Bulls of Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar.

With the drivers' championship already won by Kimi Antonelli, second place in the standings is still up for grabs.

Verstappen holds that position and is 17 points clear of George Russell, who moved back up to third place and one point ahead of Lewis Hamilton following his P4 at Interlagos.

Mercedes were also crowned constructors' champions in Brazil to move level with Williams on nine titles.

Lights out for Sunday's 50-lap race on the Las Vegas Strip is at 04:00 GMT (20:00 on Saturday local time).

Commentary of the race will be available across BBC Radio 5 Live, 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app.

You can also ask your smart speaker to "play 5 Live", for example.

Make sure to listen to every episode of the Chequered Flag podcast. For the first time this year, the post-race show for every grand prix is available to watch on BBC iPlayer and YouTube. , external

The weather forecast for Las Vegas looks dry and settled across the three days of track action.

Saturday's qualifying session and Sunday's grand prix both take place at night on the famous Strip, with conditions set to be clear with light winds and temperatures about 12C.

items.title: Antonelli fastest but penalty leaves Verstappen on pole
items.content: <article>Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli is fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a grid penalty hands pole position to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.</article>
items.lbText:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli was fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a grid penalty will hand pole position to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Antonelli, running at the back of the pack of cars in qualifying and maximising his tow, beat Verstappen by 0.258 seconds.

But the new world champion has a five-place grid penalty for using more than permitted number of engine components and will start sixth.

The Italian's team-mate George Russell was just 0.073secs behind Verstappen and will start alongside the Dutchman on the front row.

McLaren's Lando Norris qualified fourth, and will start third, ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

Both Ferraris were eliminated in the second session and qualified 11th and 12th with Charles Leclerc ahead of Lewis Hamilton.

Each will be promoted a place by a 10-place penalty for McLaren's Oscar Piastri, who qualified seventh.

Racing Bulls' rookie Arvid Lindblad, sixth fastest, is the last driver to be promoted as a result of Antonelli's penalty.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson will start seventh with Alpine's Pierre Gasly eighth and Franco Colapinto ninth.

Drivers limited to 27 laps for tyres in Qatar

Antonelli's final run did not start auspiciously as he and Russell became tangled up with the Alpines and Racing Bulls as they sought the best track position to optimise the slipstream effect.

Antonelli ended up the last driver to run and made it to the line with only one second to spare before the chequered flag, one second behind Lindblad.

Normally, being so close to the car in front would be a compromise but in Las Vegas it magnified the tow effect and Antonelli leapt to the front. "That was all the tow," he said over the radio after being told he was on pole.

"Starting the lap, I was only one second behind the car in front and I thought I was screwed," he said. "But the tow is so powerful here."

Verstappen, who has won two of the three Las Vegas Grands Prix, said: "I have been struggling with some weird issues that were also in the car in Brazil and just trying to get my head around how to deal with that.

"In qualifying we managed to make it work. Had a solid qualifying. My first lap in qualifying was pretty much as good as it could be with the tow, so to be on the front row is good for us.

"It was solid in the corners, and you have a bit of dirty air, but it is insane how much you gain on the straights."

Russell had looked in the running for the pole, but was happy with his session despite missing out.

"Overall it's been a very solid session and a solid day," he said.

"I wanted to be on pole but I am probably more pleased with the performance than in Mexico when I was on the front row.

"Kimi did a great job and he probably thought it wasn't going to work out so well being so close but with the tow it worked out."

Leclerc and Hamilton were separated by 0.056 seconds and both had tales of woe that explained their early exit - but very different ones.

Leclerc said: "Just a very poor qualifying. We are losing one second in the straights which makes it difficult enough already, and then I did a mistake when I had to put the lap in in Q2, following multiple mistakes we have done as a team and this we need to look at because it builds a lot of frustration that doesn't help.

"But in the end the mistake is on me and I will look at that."

Hamilton added: "It was a nightmare. Just low grip, felt like the tyres weren't working, had some damage on the floor that appeared out of nowhere and was losing 0.3-0.4secs and then had a deployment issue that lost us 0.6secs and with that we were nowhere, and I had no-one ahead of me. That wasn't great. So everything wasn't great.

"We knew we would struggle a bit here but maybe more than we anticipated."

items.title: Drivers limited to 27 laps for tyres in Qatar
items.content: <article>Formula 1 drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at next weekend's Qatar Grand Prix.</article>
items.lbText:
Formula 1 drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at next weekend's Qatar Grand Prix.

The decision is caused by concern over the integrity of the Pirelli tyres on the high-speed Lusail track, which has a series of demanding, long-duration corners.

It means teams will have to make at least two pit stops during the 57-lap grand prix, as was the case last year.

The limit applies on a single set of tyres whenever it is used across sessions.

So mileage done in practice or qualifying, for example, would limit the number of laps that could be done on a set of tyres in the race.

Pirelli said the limit was longer then last year's 25 laps because of the reduced downforce levels of the 2026 cars compared with 2025.

"The increase has been made possible by the lower load levels recorded so far on the current generation of cars and by a further reinforcement of the tyre construction," a statement said.

Last year, the limit led to a major strategic error by McLaren, who lost a win because they failed to pit under a safety car period when everyone else did.

It is the third time in four years Pirelli has imposed a tyre-duration limit at Qatar, where running wide over flat kerbs in addition to the high-speed nature of the track is especially demanding for the tyres.

Pirelli described the decision as a "precautionary measure" that was "linked to the unique characteristics of the Lusail circuit, which is particularly demanding in terms of energy loads, thermal stress and tread wear".

In terms of the way the limit will be imposed, the statement said: "Laps will be counted cumulatively across all track sessions, including any laps completed under the safety car or virtual safety car.

"As far as the grand prix is concerned, all laps completed from the start signal to the chequered flag will count towards the total.

"Reconnaissance laps, formation laps and any laps completed after the end of the race will not be included.

"In all other track sessions, any lap that has been started but not completed will nevertheless be counted as a full lap.

"Should a team assemble a tyre set using tyres that have covered different mileages, the tyre with the highest lap count will determine the mileage attributed to that set."

items.title: F1 bosses agree V8 engines deal from 2030
items.content: <article>Formula 1 bosses reach a deal that means V8 turbo hybrid engines will replace the current controversial units in 2030.</article>
items.lbText:
Formula 1 bosses are close to a deal that will see V8 turbo hybrid engines replace the current controversial engines in 2030.

McLaren chief executive officer Zak Brown said an "agreement in principle" had been reached by engine manufacturers and F1 bosses on the new rules.

These will be for a 2.1-litre V8 turbo engine with a smaller electrical element than this year, as first revealed by BBC Sport last month.

Some details remain to be resolved but the main core of the rules has been agreed.

The electrical element will be for a maximum power output of 200kW - compared with 350kW this year.

But only half of that will be available at all times, with the remaining half used only for an overtake mode.

A key element of the rules will be to remove the issue of energy starvation that has been criticised by the drivers this year for taking away "pure" racing.

But the overall power output of the engines will be similar to now.

The combustion engine will have about 780bhp, while 200kW is 270bhp.

That means a total power output of 1,050bhp in overtake mode or just over 900bhp in standard running.

Brown said: "Everyone is very, very excited. Now it's about kind of dotting the i's and crossing the t's.

"I'm excited for the new engines, I think everyone will be, the power units. But there's a lot more also going on to continue to evolve the sport. So, between the FIA and Formula 1, they're doing a great job."

Russell fastest in Las Vegas practice after rain

How to follow Las Vegas Grand Prix on the BBC

Alpine executive director Flavio Briatore said: "We have the agreement, basically. It's not signed, but it looks like everybody's agreed to 2030 V8s, and I'm very happy.

"It's the right way to go. We need an engine with a lot of noise, and a simple engine, and we need to be racing with that."

The ruleset amounts to a compromise reached by manufacturers after FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially pushed for a naturally aspirated engine without turbo or electrical components.

But these were required to reduce overall fuel consumption, and therefore weight at the start of races.

That means Ben Sulayem's desire for a return to the loud volumes of the previous V8 era from 2006 to 2013 will not be achieved. The engines are expected to sound similar to now.

This was important because a significant increase in engine noise would have put at threat some races in city centres that are commercially important to F1, such as Miami and Las Vegas.

The 2.1-litre capacity has been arrived at because it amounts to adding to two cylinders to the current 1.6-litre V6 blocks, with the aim of reducing development costs.

Cars are expected to start races with about 110-120kg of fuel, up from about 100kg now. A total weight limit of 150kg for the power-units will be imposed, down by about 30kg from the current engines.

There will be a fuel energy flow limit to keep the power of the combustion engine under control, and a budget cap figure for engines set at $190m (£145m) per year.

As part of negotiations, General Motors, backers of the Cadillac team, will delay the production of its new engine until 2030. It had been scheduled for 2029.

In return, GM will lose its voting rights on current engine rules and be classified as a new manufacturer from 2030.

The team will continue to use Ferrari customer engines through 2029.

Cadillac F1 chief executive officer Dan Towriss said: "For a period of time, we were working on both. So, they've already got a V6 base to build off of, and working towards the V8.

"There are a number of designs that are in motion now, and so there's a lot of good foundation for what we're trying to build and the direction we're headed in."

items.title: Russell fastest in Las Vegas practice after rain
items.content: <article>Mercedes' George Russell topped a second practice session at the Las Vegas Grand Prix run on a wet but slowly drying track.</article>
items.lbText:
Mercedes driver George Russell topped a second practice session at the Las Vegas Grand Prix run on a wet but slowly drying track.

Russell, competing with Red Bull's Max Verstappen for second in the championship in the final three races of the year, set his time right at the end of the session.

The same applied to Alpine's Pierre Gasly, who went second, 0.071 seconds behind Russell, with a lap even later the Briton's.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, the main pace-setter throughout the session, was third fastest ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

The Frenchman had a faster lap ruined when he was blocked by Haas' Oliver Bearman at the end of the Strip.

Russell said: "We know in the wet it is different every lap, every session, realistically we were not the fastest today.

"McLaren looked exceptionally fast. Charles looked very fast at points, we just got the lap in when the track was at its driest and Norris didn't run.

"We have some things to understand because Kimi and I were very competitive in the wet last week and both of us were off the pace."

Hadjar added: "It was good fun but I don't think it's very useful for tomorrow. Just shaking down the car."

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was fifth, ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and the second McLaren of Lando Norris, who was fastest in the wettest early part of the session.

New world champion Kimi Antonelli was eighth fastest, ahead of Alpine's Franco Colapinto and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso.

F1 bosses close to V8 engines deal from 2030

The art of protection - inside an F1 helmet factory

Verstappen did not run until late in the session but was complaining about a problem with his engine.

Perhaps surprisingly given the conditions, the session was incident-free, although it was stopped briefly in the closing stages to recover a plastic bag that had blown on to the circuit.

Williams driver Alex Albon said: "I'm always surprised when I see no crashes. Trickiest track of the year, lowest grip of the year, these cars and a wet track is a lot of sliding."

The forecast is for dry weather for the rest of the weekend and the teams' focus will be on understanding the tyres, with warm-up so difficult in the cold conditions and with low loads going through the tyres.

This issue is exacerbated this year with the new 'straight-line mode', in which the wings open to reduce drag on the straights to aid energy recovery.

Russell said: "It's always a challenge here in Vegas but the added challenge this year with the nature of the cars, the SM zones everywhere, you're not putting any vertical load in the tyres so they are getting substantially cooler in the straight than in the previous years and they were already pretty cool."

In the first practice session, no driver completed a timed lap because the track was extremely wet and teams preferred to save their limited allocation of wet-weather tyres.

Hamilton said: "It wasn't a great day just sitting around waiting. You can't really test much in those conditions. And everything you learn from today you have to forget because tomorrow is supposed to be dry, so we kind of start from tomorrow.

"Everyone is (going in blind). No-one has put the slicks on, so we will have to react quickly. Hopefully, it's not bad and we are there or thereabouts."

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live and 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

Piastri will have a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine-part allowance this season.

The new internal combustion engine the Australian needs as a result of a failure at the Mexico City Grand Prix two races ago is his fifth of the season - only four are permitted.

Piastri and team-mate Norris will also use the latest turbo Mercedes have produced under F1's engine upgrade scheme but that comes penalty-free.

That is not the case for Williams' Carlos Sainz, who will take the new turbo but it is his fifth of the season, so he also has a 10-place penalty which team-mate Alex Albon avoids despite also fitting the new turbo.

At the factory team, only Antonelli will use the new turbo. The team decided it was not worth Russell having it as it would have given him a 15-place grid penalty.

The turbo provides only a small performance upgrade and is more aimed at expanding the engine's useability for the 2027 season.

Bearman also has a grid penalty for engine changes and is set to start from the back of the grid.

items.title: The art of protection - inside an F1 helmet factory
items.content: <article>Inside the extraordinary world of Formula 1 helmets, where precision engineering, personal expression and life-saving technology join forces.</article>
items.lbText:
As soft, instrumental opera music plays in the background of a precise temperature-controlled room in northern Italy, Thomaso is using a children's toy ball and hairdryer to perform his meticulous work.

Hugely focused, in a crisp white coat, he moulds a precious sticky black material over and over again for up to six hours.

One day, his fastidiousness may save the life of one of the best athletes in the world.

The room Thomaso works in is called "the magic shop". Its motto? 'One man, one shell.'

Much of what happens inside is top secret. What we can say is the black material Thomaso is working with is a blend of carbon fibre that has to be stored at exactly -16°C. He moulds it into a secret form, layer by layer, after which the entire unit is baked in a vacuum bag at a set pressure at 120C for three-and-a-half hours.

The handmade products he is working on are personally chosen by their clients - for their safety features, as well as comfort, practicality and look.

Thomaso's colleague Sven travels the world between February and December to keep those clients happy. A different country almost every week, with a reliable weather forecast almost as important as a large allowance of hand luggage.

Together with 32 colleagues, Thomaso and Sven work for one of the four leading manufacturers of F1 helmets.

They produce sophisticated engineering masterpieces, and works of art.

"Our philosophy is to make the best product for the best drivers," says chief executive Alberto Dall'Oglio.

In the early days of grand prix racing, protection was rudimentary. Drivers often wore little more than leather flying caps, goggles and - eventually - relatively basic open-face helmets.

Safety standards were inconsistent, materials primitive and the consequences of an accident frequently devastating.

According to the official F1 website, Giuseppe Farina - the first winner of an F1 race and first world champion - competed wearing nothing more than "his trusty cloth cap, two pairs of goggles (he wore the spare pair round his neck), cotton dungarees, leather boots and leather gloves".

The arrival of the full-face helmet in the late 1960s marked a defining moment. Bell introduced its pioneering Star model in 1966, and Dan Gurney became the first driver to race in a full-face helmet in 1968. The face - previously exposed to flying debris, fire and impact - finally had meaningful protection.

Progress was painfully slow, and motorsport's darkest moments repeatedly exposed the limitations of the technology.

In 1976, Niki Lauda 's Ferrari erupted into flames at the Nurburgring. His helmet came loose, leaving his head exposed to the fire. He survived, but suffered severe burns and lifelong injuries. The accident became a defining lesson in the importance of helmet retention, fire resistance and the protection of the driver's entire head.

The tragic deaths of Roland Ratzenberger and Ayrton Senna at Imola in 1994, followed by Jules Bianchi's fatal accident at Suzuka in 2014, demonstrated even increasingly sophisticated helmets could not eliminate every danger.

Ratzenberger suffered a fatal basilar skull fracture; Senna succumbed to multiple fractures of the skull base, after a strut from the suspension pierced his helmet.

Bianchi's accident exposed the vulnerability of drivers' heads to heavy external impacts. Helmets are only one part of a much wider safety system, which now includes stronger survival cells, the Hans device and the halo.

In 2004, the FIA introduced its new helmet safety standard, requiring advanced carbon-fibre construction to deliver greater strength, improved impact protection and reduced weight for F1 drivers.

At Bahrain's Sakhir circuit in 2020, Romain Grosjean's Haas split apart against the barriers and burst into flames. After 28 seconds trapped in the wreckage, he emerged with burns to his hands and ankles. His Bell helmet, fire-resistant equipment and the halo were instrumental in saving his life - a powerful testament to decades of safety innovation and engineering.

"Today's helmets are withstanding up to 30 seconds at 700, even 800, degrees," says Dall'Oglio. "Then they have to self-extinguish within 15 seconds."

Dall'Oglio is the CEO of Schuberth Performance, Thomaso an engineer and Sven a racing service technician, working trackside at more than 400 grands prix, preparing helmets and visors for rain, sun or floodlights.

Needing to avoid any impact on the helmets, he must carry them - sometimes five or six at a time - to races.

Schuberth, a German firm, has a long history in head protection. Founded in 1922, the company began making industrial products before moving into helmet linings in the late 1920s, then mining and motorcycle helmets in the 1950s.

With its HQ in Magdeburg and F1 helmet production in Schio, northern Italy, it produces special helmets for military forces - made of Kevlar, and some of a similar carbon - in the same factory as the F1 helmets.

Its motorsport credentials grew considerably around the turn of the millennium.

Following Michael Schumacher's British Grand Prix accident in 1999, Schuberth developed a new generation of racing helmets, subsequently worn by Schumacher and other leading drivers.

Of the current drivers, four-time world champion Max Verstappen is the most prominent to wear a Schuberth helmet. He is joined by Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar, Cadillac's Sergio Perez, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Arvid Lindblad at Racing Bulls.

Dall'Oglio's team hand-makes about 250 helmets a year.

An F1 helmet is a remarkable marriage of science and aesthetics.

Constructed using advanced composite materials, including carbon fibre, it must be exceptionally strong while remaining light enough to minimise strain on a driver's neck.

Visors, ventilation systems, fire-resistant linings, communication equipment, a straw-like drinks system and carefully designed retention mechanisms all contribute to its performance.…

items.title: F1 to introduce full-time race stewards from 2027
items.content: <article>Formula 1's governing body the FIA is to introduce permanent race stewards from the 2027 season.</article>
items.lbText:
Formula 1's governing body the FIA is to introduce permanent race stewards from the 2027 season.

The move follows consistent calls from grand prix drivers for the change because of criticisms of inconsistency of decisions regarding penalties for on-track incidents.

The FIA said in a statement that it would begin recruiting permanent stewards, and was planning a "phased introduction" during the 2027 season.

The FIA statement added: "The introduction of dedicated full-time stewards to the FIA's flagship championship will provide continuity and expertise within the stewarding structure, further advancing the FIA's commitment to fairness through the ongoing review and continuous improvement of sporting regulations and stewarding guidelines.

"It will also allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making."

It said that the use of driver stewards, usually an ex-F1 driver, would continue, "recognising the invaluable expertise they bring".

The plan is for "a small number" of full-time stewards to be recruited during 2027 and the group to be expanded from 2028.

"Existing FIA stewards will continue to play a vital role, contributing their experience within a mixed roster of full-time and part-time stewards for the foreseeable future," the statement said.

In reality, the move is not a major step on from the current situation, where a small number of stewards are rotated around races.

Each grand prix has a group of four stewards, one of which is an ex-driver.

Current drivers have often referenced the fact that they had repeatedly complained during briefings with FIA officials that rulings on driver standards and racing errors were not applied on a consistent basis.

Last year, Williams driver Carlos Sainz, a director of drivers' body the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, said: "F1 and the FIA all agree that [permanent stewards] should be the way forward, where at least two of the three stewards are permanent and we have one rotational for teaching purposes."

The decision follows the opening of an FIA race operations centre at F1's Biggin Hill headquarters in south London.

The FIA has in recent years received increased income from F1 - which provides the majority of its funding - on the basis that this would be applied to improving officialdom and rule-making.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula 1 World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport."

items.title: Verstappen 'trusts' F1 over Middle East decision
items.content: <article>Max Verstappen says he trusts in Formula 1 after their decision to end the season in the Middle East, despite the ongoing conflicts in the area. </article>
items.lbText:
Max Verstappen says he "trusts" Formula 1 has made the right decision in pressing ahead with the final two races of the season in the Middle East.

Last week, F1 stood down preparations for a substitute race at Imola in Italy if the events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi could not be held because of ongoing conflicts in the area.

The sport will now conclude the season in the Middle East, unless the situation deteriorates before the Qatar event on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December.

Verstappen said: "I trust F1 and FIA to make the right call on that, right?

"I don't have all the intel. I'm not an officer. I just hope that they make the right call on that. And that's all that you can rely on, really.

"They also send over their findings and understanding. So I trust them."

Verstappen had previously voiced his opposition to ending the season in the Middle East.

"Normally I am happy to go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but you know, when there is a war nearby, and if some of the countries are in conflict with each other, then I think we shouldn't go," Verstappen said in September.

The Red Bull driver's fresh remarks reflect a uniform public stance in F1 on the situation, even though there are widespread misgivings among personnel about travelling to the Middle East in the context of the two conflicts in the area.

Last Sunday Iran targeted a US military base in Bahrain with a drone attack for the second time in three days, the latest salvo in the war launched against the country by the US and Israel in February.

And Houthi rebels in Yemen are advancing in their war against the Saudi-backed government of the country.

Missile attacks from the Houthis into Saudi Arabia are threatening that country's chances of hosting the second grand prix of next season, which is scheduled for 19-21 March.

McLaren's Lando Norris said that while he is "fine" with the decision to race, he is concerned about the "big team" behind him.

"I have my friend's wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there and then going on to Qatar and then Abu Dhabi," he added.

"But it's not about me. It's a lot more people. It's the fans, it's the team personnel, so the question is for them, more than I would say it is for myself."

Mercedes driver George Russell said he has "no hesitation" in racing and that while he's "sure some people have their reservations" he doesn't "know of anyone who's concerned".

"I know people who live in the region and they said it quite bluntly, if they didn't feel comfortable they wouldn't be there with their families," he said.

"When you look around the world there are a lot of terrible things going on.

"You've just got to trust in the people. If they say it's safe, then you trust in them. F1 aren't stupid and I'm sure there's plans A, B, C, D, etc. So fingers crossed it'll all be fine."

MotoGP, which is owned by the same US group as F1, held a race in Qatar last weekend without problems.

F1, which has significant commercial links with the Middle East, has been closely monitoring the situation and has been advised by security officials and government figures in the Gulf and Europe that the races can go ahead, and there is no official advice against travelling to Qatar or Abu Dhabi.

F1 said in a statement last week that it was still prepared to cancel the two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi if the situation deteriorated.

"If the situation develops negatively in the coming weeks before the events in the Middle East, we will not hesitate to do the right thing and the safety of everyone will always be the priority," an F1 spokesperson said on Tuesday.

items.title: No trust problem with Ferrari team - Hamilton
items.content: <article>Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari are "super united" despite two recent incidents in which the British driver ignored a team call to pit for fresh tyres.</article>
items.lbText:
Lewis Hamilton says there is "definitely not" a trust problem between him and his Ferrari team.

The seven-time champion has twice in the past four races ignored a call to pit for fresh tyres, both times to his competitive disadvantage.

The most recent time, in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on 8 November, Hamilton stayed out on worn slick tyres in worsening rain and ended up spinning before pitting on the next lap.

Before this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, Hamilton spoke positively of his relationship with his race engineer Carlo Santi.

"We're constantly working on our communication," said Hamilton, who had a different race engineer last year.

"It's been a lot better this year. Carlos (sic) has done an amazing job. And those particular two times, particularly the last time, was just I didn't have the information I needed. I got the call right at the last minute.

"We'll just continue to work on the processes. We're super united in what's working, in the right direction."

The previous time Hamilton ignored a call to pit was in Singapore, when he decided to stay out during a virtual safety car period. He later apologised .

At the following race in Austin, he explained that he was "always looking at ways to win, always looking at doing potentially something different. And I wanted to be on a different strategy, not just the same strategy as Charles (Leclerc), where we just follow each other".

Ferrari's Hamilton-Leclerc problem - and other F1 stories to follow

'We've got big problems' - Hamilton says Ferrari need 'serious talks'

Verstappen 'trusts' F1 over Middle East decision

Hamilton and Leclerc both insisted that relations between the pair were good after clear-the-air talks in Brazil following a disagreement at the previous race in Mexico, where a tangle on the first lap led to them throwing away a potential one-two and handing victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Hamilton said in Las Vegas on Wednesday: "Charles is a great driver. The detail we went into about stuff like that in terms of when we close the visor, it's very clear we understand each other.

"We understand each other's boundaries and the ultimate goal, which is to get the best result for the team.

"So I don't feel that that will be a problem going forward. I have no concerns or worries about racing him, and I don't think he does with me either."

Leclerc said: "The discussion went very well. Very, very quickly, after a few sentences already, the tension that was there was not there anymore, and it was all fine.

"We both work in the direction of having that second place in the constructors' championship. The second place in the constructors' is important.

"It's also true that we've got a relatively big margin behind, which doesn't mean we need to minimise that, and we still have to work as a team. But what is really important for me now is to try and win before the end of the season and win the race."

He added that "everything has been taken out of proportion" but he is "kind of used to it" have been at Ferrari since 2019.

"Of course, the goal is not always to agree, and that will never happen," he added.

"We can have different opinions, and that was the case, for example, in Mexico. But just the fact of speaking eased all tensions, and we were completely fine with it.

"It's not that we had to speak for an hour, even though it ended up lasting an hour, just because we had a good time and we started speaking about also many other things in trying to bring the team and to help the team go forward.

"But the discussion about the tension was like maybe five or 10 minutes, and then the air was clean, and that's it."

items.title: Bottas' stay at Cadillac confirmed for 2027
items.content: <article>Valtteri Bottas is retained by Cadillac for the 2027 Formula 1 season.</article>
items.lbText:
Valtteri Bottas has been retained by Cadillac for the 2027 Formula 1 season.

The future of the 37-year-old Finn had been in doubt as the American team endure a difficult maiden campaign.

To date, they have failed to collect a point in either the drivers' or constructors' championship.

However, two-time championship runner-up Bottas will race again with them next year.

"I'm excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027," said Bottas, who is preparing for Sunday's Las Vegas Grand Prix.

"We knew building a new Formula One team from the ground up wasn't going to be easy, but that's exactly what makes this challenge so special.

"We've laid the foundations, we're learning and improving, and there's still plenty more to come. I'm hungry for more, and I believe in what we're building together. The story is only just getting started."

The news follows the recent announcement that Mexican Sergio Perez, 36, will also be remaining with Cadillac until 2029 after signing a contract extension.

Cadillac had been considering whether to promote their American reserve driver, Colton Herta, into Bottas' seat.

The 26-year-old former Indycar driver has earned enough points to apply for the superlicence required to drive in F1 through his outings in practice this year.

But the feeling was that there was no obvious upgrade to Bottas and that the Finn had not been given a fair run in what has been a difficult debut season for Cadillac beset by reliability problems and lack of pace.

The team decided that they needed stability for their second season, and that the experience provided by Perez and Bottas, who have both won grands prix, was as important as ever.

Herta had given up his seat in Indycar to drive in Formula 2 this season with the idea of preparing himself for F1.

However, he has had a difficult season and lies 19th in the championship with two races remaining.

Herta now faces a decision as to what to do in 2027.

Cadillac are still open to the idea of him graduating to F1, perhaps in 2028, but it is not clear where he may race next year while he waits to see whether that opportunity arises.

TWG, the US consortium which runs Cadillac, has other teams in other categories for which Herta could race alongside any F1 reserve role that might be on offer.

One of the options would involve a return to Indycar, or Herta could perhaps move into endurance racing.

items.title: Cowboy boots, cocktails and casinos - how do three US grands prix compare?
items.content: <article>F1 struggled to establish itself in the United States, but now hosts three grands prix. We compare the merits of Austin, Miami and Las Vegas.</article>
items.lbText:
"The picnic blanket that you'd happily sit on in Austin will get confiscated by security at Miami and will end up wrapped around you in the chill of a Vegas night."

Cadence Kim from Dallas lives the reality of being an avid Formula 1 fan in the United States, in the three diverse locations the sport now frequents. She will be among the 300,000 spectators around the iconic Las Vegas Strip this weekend.

Las Vegas joined the F1 calendar in 2023, a year after Miami, while Austin has been home to the United States Grand Prix since 2012.

Kim has put in the hard yards travelling across the Atlantic to witness F1 in its European heartland. Now she is reaping the rewards of owners Liberty Media investing heavily in the three US races, which have all recently been awarded new long-term contracts.

"Following F1 from the US used to mean accepting a massive barrier to entry," Kim explains.

"It meant setting an early alarm and trying to explain to room mates why you were yelling at 20 rich men driving funny-looking cars very quickly. It was more of a niche sport with no natural gathering places for a community to watch. What bar is open at that time?

"Having three domestic races has changed everything. It has shifted F1 from a purely broadcast experience into something tangible. It becomes a week-long experience where a fan gets to engage with a like-minded community, attend parties in the evening, and do a meet-and-greet. You can walk a track, sit in a grandstand, purchase the overpriced merch, hear the engines and literally feel a part of something."

The community Kim is attached to is the ATX GP Club, formed in Austin by Maria Rodriguez and Julia Wezio, where watch parties help fans learn more about the sport and the drivers. With the longest running of the US races on their doorstep, at the Circuit of the Americas, she's ideally placed to compare all three venues for the fan experience.

"Vegas is a party," exclaims Kim. "The Nevada desert gets cold at night, so the cowboy hat doesn't make the trip, but socks, a hoodie and gloves do.

"Many of the teams have hotel partnerships so lobbies become team activation zones, and you might end up sharing an elevator with an engineer. The fan flow is well managed with everyone being funnelled through specific pedestrian walkways, but if you do have a ticket to watch the race at the track you are limited to staying only in that one specific zone.

"Vegas is known for its dining but that doesn't make it to the track. Ticketing forces you to consider some pretty rigid trade-offs. For example, sitting at Turn One means missing the musical artists and activations by the Sphere.

"As for Austin, you aren't restricted to a single assigned area but can walk almost the entire perimeter of the track. With each of the three races you get a local vibe integrated into the entertainment. It's not an artificially manufactured aesthetic in Austin, you're getting real Texas BBQ, smoked brisket and bedazzled cowboy hats.

"I've been once to Miami and would not consider going back unless it became a night race. The South Florida sun bakes both the track and the attendees during the daytime. Preparing for an outdoor trek is the best mindset. Treat it like a multi-day hike where you'll be logging 30,000 steps each day so comfortable shoes and water with electrolyte packets are a must."

The excitement level of racing at the Las Vegas Grand Prix in its opening three years has been as bright as the neon lights on the Strip. The debut race in 2023 was an instant classic, with the lead changing hands five times, and drama all the way to the line as Charles Leclerc overtook Sergio Perez for second place, behind winner Max Verstappen.

It was instant payback for F1, who had invested more than £500m in buying land and promoting the event. Despite complaints from some local residents and businesses over the disruption to the city streets, the gamble has paid dividends, according to Vegas-based podcast host and nine-time Le Mans 24 Hours driver Justin Bell.

"I was telling people, 'just wait'. It's like a big piece of Ikea furniture – once you do it once, it's so much quicker and more efficient the next time," Bell tells BBC Sport.

"The promoters did listen to the locals and worked out ways to get them involved, by offering discounted tickets and attempting to minimise the disruption. Let's face it, Las Vegas exists for one reason and that is to entertain visitors, and with the extraordinary economic impact it has I am sure the pros outweigh the cons for almost everyone involved."

That economic impact has been valued at $3.2bn for the Southern Nevada region over the three years, with each of the 175,000 visitors from outside Las Vegas spending an average of $2,400 on non-racing activities, according to figures from the 2024 race.

Bell, who presents the Drive to Wynn podcast from the luxury resort on the Strip, and used to guide celebrities like Drew Barrymore and Steve Carell in race cars on the Jay Leno Show, thinks Vegas has the perfect opportunity to position itself as the premier US race, despite it being the youngest.

"Vegas has such a leg up on the other two locations as a global entertainment hub, that aligns so well with the direction that F1 is heading as a brand," he says. "Miami is sexy and in theory has much going for it, but the track itself isn't in Miami so there are the usual inconveniences in terms of transportation.

"In contrast, I always recommended Austin to F1 newcomers as a track to visit first, because it is a purpose-built facility that is so easy to spectate at, with tons of room to walk around and watch cars from every angle all while eating a hotdog.

"From the first laps from 2023, it became evident that the Vegas track design was going to be great for F1. The mix of tight corners with that long straight down the iconic Strip invites breathtaking overtaking. Each successive year gets better."…

items.title: Alonso to drive in Dakar Rally for Aston Martin
items.content: <article>Two-time Formula 1 world champion Fernando Alonso will head Aston Martin's attempt to win the Dakar Rally in January 2027.</article>
items.lbText:
Two-time Formula 1 world champion Fernando Alonso will lead Aston Martin's attempt to win the Dakar Rally in January 2027.

The 45-year-old Spaniard, who drives for the British team in Formula 1, previously contested the prestigious rally raid event in 2020 for Toyota.

Aston Martin have struggled in the first year of F1's new regulations in the Adrian Newey-designed AMR26 car.

Alonso sits 17th in the drivers' championship, team-mate Lance Stroll 22nd, and the team 10th in the constructors', only ahead of last-placed Cadillac.

Alonso, who recently signed a new Aston Martin deal and is widely regarded as one of the biggest talents in motorsport history, is joined in the Dreadnought by co-driver Marc Coma.

Coma is a five-time winner of the Dakar on a motorbike and was also Alonso’s co-driver in 2020.

The two other cars will be driven by nine-time world rally champion Sebastien Loeb of France and current world rally raid champion Lucas Moraes of Brazil.

"After deciding to continue racing in Formula 1 with Aston Martin, I thought carefully about Dakar," said Alonso. "In the end, the decision became simple. I wanted to embrace the challenge completely.

"I have enormous respect for this race and the specialists who have mastered it. Having Marc alongside me again is very important, and with Aston Martin, Prodrive, Sebastien and Lucas we have an exceptional team."

It will be Aston's first involvement in the famously gruelling and dangerous race and they will go up against more established Dakar teams such as Toyota and KTM.

Aston's Dakar machines will be prepared by Prodrive - who had considerable success in rallying with Subaru in the 1990s and 2000s.

Despite challenges on the tarmac in F1, Aston have enjoyed much-improved performances in the World Endurance Championship this year, including at the season finale at Monza last month through the 007 Valkyrie car driven by Tom Gamble and Harry Tincknell.

Alonso could even drive the Valkyrie at the famous Le Mans 24 Hours in 2027 - F1 commitments permitting - where he won with Toyota in 2018 and 2019.

The 2027 Dakar Rally will begin in Portugal on 9 January and after 12 stages end in Morocco on 23 January.

Last month it was announced Dakar would be switched from Saudi Arabia following the unrest in the Middle East because of the Iran war.

The race, which also includes other classifications of cars, as well as lorries and motorbikes, was traditionally held between Paris and Dakar from the late 1970s, but the route has been adjusted over the years for promotional and safety reasons.

Alonso's previous Dakar brought a 13th-place finish. A couple of crashes caused by inexperience of the event delayed him, but a second-place finish on one stage showed his pace and potential.

"Formula 1 remains my priority," he said. "But I am a racing driver, and challenges like this are why I love competing. I'm looking forward to seeing what we can achieve."

items.title: Why Hamilton is key to Bearman's future - F1 Q&A
items.content: <article>BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the Las Vegas Grand Prix.</article>
items.lbText:
The 2026 Formula 1 season closes with three races in consecutive weekends, the first of them a night race in Las Vegas.

With the drivers' and constructors' titles won by Kimi Antonelli and Mercedes respectively, there remains a close contest over who finishes second in the drivers' championship.

Before the race along the Vegas' Strip, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

Is Ollie Bearman's career in danger of stalling by being at Haas and stuck in the Ferrari bottleneck? He obviously has the talent to be a world championship contender but being stuck at the back of the grid can't be doing his career any good. - Dave

Oliver Bearman has still not been confirmed as a Haas driver for 2027, even though both parties say that's what they want.

From Bearman's point of view, it's not hard to see why he might be asking a few questions about his future.

He is a member of the Ferrari driver academy and they show no sign of wanting him not to be, but at the same time they are not showing much sign of wanting to promote him to the senior team.

In that sense, Bearman's future hangs to a degree on Lewis Hamilton's.

Hamilton is talking about staying in F1 at least until 2030, which would mean a new contract at the end of next year, presumably with Ferrari.

But will Ferrari keep him? That is unknown, amid what has undoubtedly been some tension between him, team-mate Charles Leclerc and the team management this season.

If Hamilton stays, Bearman would be within his rights to ask how they see his future, and to ask for the chance to look for opportunities elsewhere.

How secure is James Vowles' position at Williams? He seems like a great guy, always very open and honest. But the fact remains that the team targeted this year for a big performance jump and they've actually gone backwards. Is Vowles running out of time? - James

Williams have had a bad season in 2026. There is no question about that.

For three years since Vowles became team principal in 2023, he had been talking about 2026 as the team's opportunity to take a significant step towards their ambitions of returning to the front.

Having finished fifth in 2025 - a result that even surprised the team - another step forward was expected this year under the new rules.

But that's not what happened. Instead, Williams have gone significantly backwards.

The car was late, too heavy and lacked downforce. Little relative progress has been made through the year and they lie ninth in the constructors' championship with three races to go and will almost certainly finish there.

All year, Vowles has been explaining that the new rules exposed pressure points in the Williams factory that he had not realised existed. Essentially, the factory systems were not able to cope with the demands being put on them.

He says they needed this experience to be able to fix them and move forwards to a better place.

A critic might question why Vowles had not realised they were there in the three years he had been leading the time up to that point.

Drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon have been unimpressed by what has happened this year.

But Vowles succeeded in getting both to stay on for at least one more season. Although whether that was because they retain belief in the team or because they did not have that many better options is a debatable point.

Asked what gave him the confidence to stay, Albon said: "This year I've been brought into a more deeper analysis of where it went wrong from last year to this year.

"So why were we late? Why was the car overweight? What were the reasons? Why did we miss the trick on even the philosophy of the car, for example?

"I'm satisfied with what those reasons are. As simple as that, really.

"At the same time, I also want to see these things materialise and I want to see these changes happen next year."

Albon admitted to there being a "deep frustration shared with the whole team that after all the efforts of prioritising this year's car, we haven't delivered a good job".

A new, lighter chassis was introduced at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. That will be carried over into next year so, as Albon puts it, "we start next year's car with a chassis that's not heavy, that's on the right foot, that we can then start focusing a lot more on not losing weight and a lot more time on aerodynamics and making the car go faster".

Through this season, Vowles has taken to publicly calling for a revision to the cost-cap rules, saying they bake in an advantage for the big teams, and wanting allowances for extra spending for others to catch up.

His critics say that those allowances are already there in one form, and that Vowles is using this as a distraction technique.

Whether his job is on the line if there is not a significant step forward for 2027 after all this is not clear. But the pressure is mounting, and he will certainly have a lot of explaining to do if there isn't.

With Max Verstappen established at Red Bull for the foreseeable future, what is Racing Bulls' real purpose: to discover Max MkII for Red Bull or simply provide a route to finding a reliable number two? Is it time Racing Bulls was allowed to operate as a genuinely independent, competitive team, rather than effectively functioning as Red Bull's driver development programme? - Michael

Racing Bulls' raison d'etre is the same as it has always been through all its name changes since Red Bull bought Minardi at the end of 2005.

That is to act as a training ground for drivers for the main Red Bull team.

It can be argued that the Red Bull young driver programme has not been especially successful.

In 20 years, the only top-line driver it has brought up through the junior categories all the way to being a success at Red Bull Racing was Daniel Ricciardo.

Sebastian Vettel was a BMW driver before Red Bull signed him, and Max Verstappen was plucked straight into F1 by Red Bull after winning a tug-of-war with Mercedes while he was in F3.…

items.title: Camara to race again for Haas in Las Vegas
items.content: <article>Rafael Camara will again race for Haas in the Las Vegas Grand Prix following the sacking of Esteban Ocon.</article>
items.lbText:
Brazilian Rafael Camara will race for the US-based Haas team for a second time at this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The 21-year-old made his debut for Haas at the previous race, the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, alongside team-mate Oliver Bearman.

Camara, who will become a full-time driver for Haas in 2027, is replacing Frenchman Esteban Ocon, who was sacked following an altercation with team principal Ayao Komatsu at last month's Mexico City Grand Prix.

The team have not confirmed who will race alongside Bearman for the final two scheduled races of the year in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Camara is the leader of the Formula 2 championship, which is also due to end its season at those two events.

Japanese Ryo Hirakawa, the Haas reserve driver who stepped in for Ocon in Mexico, will drive in first practice in Las Vegas in Bearman's car.

Komatsu said: "In Brazil, our 2027 recruit Rafa Camara made his debut under extremely challenging conditions and showed us and the world why we signed him for 2027.

"We're looking forward to building on that for his second race weekend with us."

Camara, who qualified 13th in Sao Paulo and finished last in demanding wet-dry conditions, said: "I'm looking forward to getting back in the car in Las Vegas.

"Brazil was a good learning experience, and now the focus is on building on that, improving step by step and making the most of every session.

"It's a new circuit for me, so there's a lot to learn, but I'll do my best to keep progressing throughout the weekend."

items.title: Formula 1's one-race wonders
items.content: <article>Making it to Formula 1 is the undoubted pinnacle of any racing driver’s career – but what became of some of those who only had one shot? </article>
items.lbText:
You've been handed the chance of a lifetime.

A chance to sit in the cockpit, on the grid, at motorsport's top table: Formula 1. The very pinnacle of everything you've strived for in your whole life.

"I sang the Grand Prix theme tune while I was sat on the grid. I thought I was watching it on telly," says Tiff Needell - one of 166 lucky or unlucky drivers, depending on your standing in motorsport, who graced an F1 race only once.

There are many reasons why a driver may only get one chance to race elite sport's fastest and most sophisticated machines, and, although F1's super subs were more of a feature in the 1960s and 1970s, the helmet-for-hire phenomenon is alive and driving in ultra-professional, modern F1.

Just ask Japan's Ryo Hirakawa, who only last month achieved his "dream" , external when he got behind the wheel of a Haas at the Mexican Grand Prix following Esteban Ocon's controversial departure from the team.

"I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy," Hirakawa said after scoring a point - admittedly, following a few demotions for others. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."

Within a week there was nothing the Toyota factory driver could do as Haas' 2027 driver Rafael Camara was drafted in for the American team early, for the rest of 2026.

Hirakawa is a reserve driver for Haas as a result of the team's association with Toyota - the Japanese being in the right place at the right time.

The percentage of F1 test and reserve drivers who make it to the grid is typically low, and those who do tend to be drafted in for one shot at very unlikely glory.

The days of the aristocrat who fancies a pootle around the track are gone, and years of preparation are required even to be standing in the pit garage.

Injuries, sponsorship fails and outright cheating are just some of the reasons why it does not work out for some hopefuls.

Needell, known better for his time behind the wheel on Top Gear and other auto TV shows, got his big break at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. But his journey to the paddock was initiated a few years earlier - in the media.

"I won a car in a magazine competition," he says. "I was the kid on the terraces, on the fences - and made it on to the grid. We had no money at all in our family, so I was a working civil engineer five days a week and a mechanic in my garage five nights a week. At the weekend I was the van driver, the mechanic and the racing driver.

"I bumbled my way up to the top of the national scene and then got offered a professional drive in Formula 3. And after two years of that I moved up into the [long since defunct] Formula 1 British championship.

"I was out at the Nurburgring trying to get an F1 drive when I got the call. I was hanging around the paddock trying to chat up an F2 team, trying to say I had a sponsor, which of course I didn't.

"Ensign called me and said: 'This weekend would you like to drive?' I rushed home from the Nurburgring in my orange Ford Capri, had half a day's test at Donington and on to qualifying for the Belgian GP at Zolder.

"I got my chance because Clay Regazzoni crashed and hurt his back at Long Beach.

"A lot of that in the olden days was due to injuries - chances would come up when someone had crashed and got injured. It was dangerous back then."

Needell was in, but this was old-school F1 where you had to pre-qualify to show you were fast enough to qualify for the Grand Prix itself.

"There was something like 30 drivers trying to pre-qualify, and somehow I made it to the back of the grid - 23rd in the Ensign. It was so much cheaper then - aluminium chassis and a Cosworth DFV engine and away you go."

While the back of the grid beckoned, a 29-year-old Needell was in very good company in the form of double world champion Emerson Fittipaldi, who was having a bad weekend in his Skol Fittipaldi car.

"I found myself on the back row of the grid, sitting by one of my big heroes. It was all a bit of a dream," says Needell.

In contrast to today's VIP treatment, Needell's parents and his girlfriend (now wife) drove to Belgium in the family car and watched from the crowd as he lined up on the grid.

"When the mechanics started the engine and left me sitting there - me and Emerson - I actually started humming the theme tune [to Fleetwood Mac's The Chain]," Needell says.

"For 12 laps I battled with Emerson for the honour of being last place at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. Then the engine broke."

A failed attempt to qualify for Monaco a week later put the brakes on his F1 dream and eventually resulted in Needell pursuing a career as a Le Mans racer and TV presenter.

Often the reason F1 careers could be so fleeting would be of a driver's own making.

Hans Heyer did not qualify for his one and only race - the 1977 German Grand Prix at Hockenheim - but he thought he would contest it anyway, starting from the pit lane for the ATS team in a car that was never supposed to be there.

The German may have achieved his dream at his home race, but it came with disqualification after he had already retired with gearbox failure on lap nine.

And what of Marco Apicella? It has taken 73 years, since Alberto Ascari triumphed, for Italy to celebrate one of its own F1 world champions in Kimi Antonelli as he secured the 2026 title in Mexico last month.

For a country and a Ferrari team so important to the sport, that is a long time to wait - and Apicella was a good example of why it may have taken a while.

Rushed in at the last minute after only two hours of testing to replace a disgruntled, if experienced, Thierry Boutsen in the underwhelming 1993 Jordan, Apicella lasted approximately 800 metres of his home race after a multi-car collision during the first lap of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.

That was the end of Apicella's F1 career and he would end up embarking on five unsuccessful attempts to win Le Mans.

So what's the best any of the one-hit wonders have done in their first and only grand prix?…

items.title: Much still to do on F1 diversity - Hamilton
items.content: <article>British Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton outlines three steps the sport must take to improve its diversity.</article>
items.lbText:
Lewis Hamilton says there is "much still to do" when it comes to increasing diversity in Formula 1.

The seven-time champion has used a report published on the five-year anniversary of establishing his Mission 44 charity , external to demand three key steps from the sport.

The campaign seeks to increase the representation of black people, women and people from lower socio-economic backgrounds in F1.

The report recognises that all parts of the industry have made steps to increase diversity.

But it said the sport did not have the data to show whether these efforts had "changed who enters, progresses and stays in motorsport".

Hamilton said: "When I walk through the paddock now, I see more women, more Black and Brown faces, more people who look like the fans in the grandstands than at any point since I started. That is heartening, and the people behind it deserve credit.

"And yet, there is much still to do. We have opened the door, but we have not yet learned to count how many people walk through it, or how many stay.

"The sport's first social impact report shows how much is happening. This report asks what it adds up to. This is a sport that measures performance to the thousandth of a second. We can measure this too."

The Mission 44 report makes three recommendations:

Measure who joins, who is promoted and who stays, and let the best practice be recognised.

Take investment in people out of the F1 cost cap and put money behind the pipeline collectively.

Publish the paid places being offered every year.

An F1 spokesperson said: "We are proud of the programmes and initiatives which help inspire the next generation of Formula 1 and how they continue to increase access and opportunity across our sport.

"Following recommendations from the Hamilton Commission, the sport signed its first ever diversity and inclusion charter in 2024, and in 2025 conducted its first ever sport-wide data gathering exercise to capture the global reach of our social impact programmes , external .

"This showed that in 2025 season alone, more than 500,000 young people engaged in education, STEM and inspiration programmes globally and over 1,000 structured skills and talent development opportunities across our sport.

"As F1 continues to grow on the global stage, so too does our ambition to deepen and evolve our social impact. We are committed, alongside the F1 teams, the FIA and broader members of our sport to continue build on this foundation and look forward to sharing the next phase of our work."

The Mission 44 report proposes that F1, governing body the FIA, the teams and the sport's main sponsors "invest at least £50m of new money over the next five years into supporting young people from underrepresented backgrounds into motorsport careers, and supporting them to stay".

It said it was not able to say whether activity related to diversity was succeeding in increasing numbers because there was "no collated data on the entire motorsports workforce, only on the 'activity and reach' of social impact programmes".

It added: "Figures are self-reported through a structured data request.

"However, we cannot see who is recruited as a result of the activity, who stays or who progresses in their career.

"The data does not record demographic details of who participated in the programmes, and teams define underrepresented groups differently, so even where numbers exist, they cannot be compared.

"The original question of the Hamilton Commission was how many Black people worked in motorsport. Five years on, the sport cannot say exactly how that number has changed."

The report recognised examples of improvement in diversity at teams who reported figures. Not all did.

Mercedes set itself a target in 2020 to improve representation of underrepresented groups in its workforce after data showed only 3% of were from minority ethnic backgrounds, and 12% were women.

After implementing training, recruitment and development processes for hiring, by 2025 Mercedes reported 20% of employees were women, 10% were from minority ethnic backgrounds, and 37% of new joiners in the first half of that year were from underrepresented groups.

McLaren publishes detailed workforce data every year and its 2025 sustainability report showed that 36% of staff identified with one or more underrepresented characteristics, against a 2030 target of 40%, and 44.8% of new starters in 2025 were from underrepresented groups.

Women make up 22% of McLaren F1's workforce and 10% of technical functions, with that latter number up from 7% the year before.

All the F1 teams, F1 itself and governing body the FIA have signed up to a diversity and inclusion charter , external .

F1 realised its first sport-wide social impact report last month and reported a series of steps to increase diversity and inclusion.

items.title: Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing in F1 crash?
items.content: <article>Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing after the Formula 1 car it was attached to crashed?</article>
items.lbText:
Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?

If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.

A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.

Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?

The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.

Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.

"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.

"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."

His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.

They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.

"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.

"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."

Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.

The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.

Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.

What happened next, though, was not part of the script.

While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.

The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.

Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.

Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.

Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.

In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.

Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.

It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.

"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.

He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.

"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.

"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."

By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.

Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.

"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.

"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.

"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."

Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.

"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.

"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.

"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."

"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.

"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].

"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.

"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."…

items.title: Lindblad and Lawson to continue at Racing Bulls
items.content: <article>Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson will continue as the drivers for Red Bull's second team Racing Bulls in 2027.</article>
items.lbText:
Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson will continue as the drivers for Red Bull's second team Racing Bulls in 2027.

Red Bull had been deciding whether to promote Bulgarian Formula 2 front-runner Nikola Tsolov in place of Lawson but have decided to spend a second season assessing their current line-up

Tsolov will be the reserve driver for both teams next season.

Team principal Alan Permane said: "I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition.

"Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we've seen the progress they've made, both individually and as a pairing."

The decision to retain both marks a break from the previous Red Bull philosophy of fast-tracking drivers through the programme.

Chequered Flag Extra: The Making of Kimi Antonelli

Racing Bulls essentially exists to find potential drivers for the main Red Bull team, so the company has tended to jettison drivers who have been given a chance and not succeeded.

That's why Lawson, 24, was considered vulnerable. He was promoted to Red Bull alongside Max Verstappen for the 2025 season only to be demoted after just two races in which he had struggled.

The New Zealander has since sought to rebuild his career and was much more convincing when he was re-promoted to Red Bull for the Dutch, Italian and Spanish Grands Prix this year while regular driver Isack Hadjar was recovering from a broken wrist.

Keeping Lawson on board for 2027 gives Red Bull a known-quality benchmark with which to continue their assessment of Lindblad, who made his debut this season.

The 19-year-old Briton has excelled at times in his rookie year but on average has been a little behind Lawson, who has out-qualified him 13 times to nine and has scored more than twice as many points.

Lawson said: "We've had a brilliant season together and the team has worked very hard to produce a fast car, which I've loved driving.

"It feels great to be part of a historic season for the team as we continue our fight for fifth place in the constructors' championship.

"I'm looking forward to carrying this moment forward with Arvid through to 2027; we're building something super positive and I'm excited by what we can achieve together."

Lindblad added: "It's been a truly special year, full of new experiences and learnings since the very first pre-season test. I'd like to thank everyone for their trust and support.

"I can't wait to get started next year, building on everything I've learned during my rookie season."

The news release announcing the pairing made no mention of Tsolov, who is expected to be retained by Red Bull in some form of reserve role in which he gains experience through work in the simulator and with testing previous cars.

items.title: Freddie Slater's 'surreal' first taste of Formula 1
items.content: <article>The rising star tells the BBC about his experience taking part in F1 practice in Mexico.</article>
items.lbText:
While Kimi Antonelli was making history as the youngest Formula 1 world champion earlier this month, a British teenager was taking his own steps to a glittering career in the sport.

Freddie Slater made his debut in the free practice sessions at both the Mexican and Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Slater, who grew up in Stratford-upon-Avon and was educated in Bromsgrove, was handed his first official F1 outing by Audi, and the 18-year-old is one of Britain's brightest motorsport prospects.

He has so far had successful seasons in karting and cars, most recently finishing runner up in the Formula 3 Championship, and told the BBC his latest experiences were "surreal".

"You're doing 350kph (217mph) into turn one at Mexico, I've never done anything like it, honestly it's just incredible," he said.

"(In) 2023, I was still in karting, then last year I was in the Formula Regional Championship which I won, and this year Formula 3."

Formula 3 is a support series organised by the FIA and competes alongside Formula 1, visiting the same tracks and racing on the same weekends.

It's an opportunity for drivers to get themselves noticed and for Slater it allowed him to become the first driver to be signed to Audi's driver development programme.

That has led to the recent outings in the team's Formula 1 cars.

"It's been great to have the support of Audi and the support of people like team principal Mattia Binotto and racing director Allan McNish.

"I didn't expect this opportunity to come so early if I'm honest. I just love speed and sitting in that F1 car was just the most surreal and incredible feeling. I've waited my whole life for this.

"I think the big difference with the F1 paddock is the amount of people, you have hundreds of people behind you, to get that car on track."

Slater's time in the car was cut short on both occasions due to mechanical problems - not uncommon for teams in practice sessions because both the driver and teams are learning the track and what setup works best. He adds that the opportunity itself to drive an F1 car was a dream come true.

"Honestly, I couldn't believe it when I was told I was getting to drive... it was just incredible getting those laps behind me with the forces and speeds involved".

Racing from a young age meant balancing exams and coursework with travelling around the world.

Slater's former headmaster, Mike Marie at Bromsgrove Preparatory School, said: "We're so proud of Freddie after having his first practice at an F1 weekend. My memories of Freddie were of him coming into school in year four with trophies bigger than he was, always incredibly talented, we wish him the best of luck on the world stage."

Slater recalls his time at school and the support he received there fondly: "I had to take prolonged absences to go racing, but also the friendships I've built up, the effort I put in at a young age."

Slater's family still live in Warwickshire and he is the oldest of five children.

"I love coming home after a busy race weekend, it's nice to unwind away from the pressure of the paddock, but also to catch up with family and friends.

"Motorsport is in my family, my dad used to race himself, my two brothers are also climbing the ladder, the youngest of which is 10 and just started karting."

Slater will now be gearing up for a season in Formula 2 with Invicta Racing, the current championship leaders. It means he will be around the paddock more often on a grand prix weekend - an opportunity he is relishing.

"Getting to Formula 1 is super difficult because the margins are so small and the drivers are at the top of their game.

"Of course I want to win a championship, that's got to be the goal every year, but it's also to develop as a driver.

"It's a tough sport in terms of how long the years are, there is so much testing, and training, that's the side people don't see."

Slater is not due on-track again until next year, however he will still be putting in the hours on the simulator and hitting the gym on a daily basis to stay fit.

With the support of Audi, he is also likely to feature in another practice session in the not-too-distant future.
